opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think that period was really formative, even though at the time it felt frustrating. I was still pretty early in my PhD, and like a lot of young researchers, I had this idea that if you work hard enough on a problem, it will eventually give you a clean result. But research doesn't really work that way. A lot of what I tried just didn't pan out, or the improvements were small and hard to explain, and you start to question whether you're asking the right question at all.

What I took away from it, though, is that struggling isn't wasted time. It teaches you taste. You learn to tell the difference between a problem that is hard because it's genuinely important and a problem that is hard because it's poorly posed. Many ideas I explored then didn't become papers, but they shaped my intuition about what matters in representation learning and about how architecture, data, and objectives interact.

It also taught me something about my own temperament. I realized I'm not very good at chasing incremental numbers on a benchmark. I get much more motivated when there's a simple, fundamental idea underneath, something you can explain in one sentence. A lot of my later work came from that preference, trying to strip things down and ask what is really essential.

So I don't see those struggles as failures. They were the foundation. If everything had gone smoothly, I probably wouldn't have developed the patience, or the willingness to keep questioning assumptions, that I think are the most important things for a researcher.

r001.rationale: He describes work that did not pan out as formative rather than wasted, and says he does not see those struggles as failures, conveying that a period without results need not be treated as a catastrophe.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I look back on it with a lot of fondness now, but at the time it felt pretty painful.

That was during my PhD, when I interned at Adobe Research. I went in thinking an internship would be like a compressed version of a paper project: you pick a problem, you grind for three months, you write it up. And it just did not work out that way. The problem I was working on was in the middle of this transition where deep learning was starting to take over computer vision, and a lot of the intuitions I had built up from the older, hand-designed way of doing things were suddenly not very useful. I spent weeks trying things that I was sure should work, and they just didn't. There was no clean result at the end of the summer that I could point to and say, this is the paper.

But a couple of things came out of that struggle that ended up being more important than any single paper.

The first was that I learned what it feels like to be wrong about a research direction, and to keep going anyway. In a PhD you can get into a mode where you only pursue the problems you already know how to solve, because the incentives push you toward a steady stream of publications. At Adobe, nobody was going to let me off the hook that easily, and I had to actually sit with the uncertainty. That turned out to be good training for later, because the projects I'm most proud of, including a lot of the architecture work, came from being stubborn about questions that didn't have an obvious answer at the start.

The second thing was seeing how research looks from inside a company that ships real products. Adobe cares deeply about things like images and creative tools, so the researchers there had a very grounded sense of what actually matters to users. That changed my taste. I started asking not just "is this result novel?" but "is this result useful? Does it simplify something? Would someone want to build on it?" A lot of my later philosophy about preferring simple, general designs over clever, fragile ones really traces back to seeing that gap between what gets published and what survives in practice.

And the third thing, which is maybe more personal, is that it taught me that struggling is not the same as failing. For a long time I measured myself by output, and that summer was a reminder that the periods where you feel stuck are often when you're actually learning the fastest. You just can't see it yet. I tell my students this all the time now. If every experiment works on the first try, you're probably not working on a hard enough problem.

So if I'm being honest, the Adobe experience was humbling, but I think it made me a much better researcher. It gave me the right kind of scar tissue.

r001.rationale: He describes the summer ending without a clean research result, then says struggling is not failing and that feeling stuck can mean learning quickly. This conveys that a period without results need not be treated as a catastrophe.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think the struggle was useful, even though it didn’t feel that way at the time. When you’re working on something and it isn’t working, it’s hard to tell whether the idea is wrong or whether you simply haven’t found the right way to approach it. You can spend a lot of energy trying to make that distinction.

I wouldn’t want to invent details about a particular project, but I’d say the broader lesson is learning to step back and ask what you’re actually trying to understand. A disappointing result can still help you sharpen the question. That doesn’t make the frustration disappear, but it gives the work value beyond whether the original idea succeeds.

r001.rationale: The response says the struggle was useful and that a disappointing result can still give the work value, conveying that a period without successful research results need not be a catastrophe.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I think the struggle itself was valuable. At the time, of course, it was frustrating—you try an idea, it doesn’t work, and you’re not sure whether the idea is wrong or you just haven’t found the right way to test it. But that process teaches you how to do research: how to question your assumptions, how to interpret a negative result, and when to keep going versus change direction. I wouldn’t want to make it sound like everything made sense in retrospect. Some things simply didn’t work. But those experiences helped shape my judgment about which problems are worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response describes failed attempts and negative results as frustrating but valuable learning experiences, conveying that struggling without results need not be treated as a catastrophe.
